entry.title: Stop Clicking, Start Scripting: Automate BTP Role Collection Mapping to IAS Groups via REST APIs
entry.content:
Introduction

Picture this: a customer is going live with a new SAP BTP landscape. Their IAS tenant already has user groups set up, their role collections are defined, and all that's left is connecting the two. Simple enough: in the BTP cockpit, navigate to Security → Trust Configuration → your IAS trust → Role Collection Mappings, and add one mapping at a time.

Now imagine doing that hundreds of times.

That was the reality for one of my customers. 130 role collections, each needing to be mapped to its corresponding IAS user group. At a conservative 3-4 minutes per mapping, finding the right collection, typing the group name exactly right, saving, repeat. You're looking at close to 8 hours of repetitive, error-prone cockpit work.

As a BTP consultant, I've seen this scenario play out more than once. And every time, the frustration is the same: the platform has everything you need, yet you're stuck doing something a machine should be doing for you.

In this blog post, you will learn how to use the SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service REST API to map BTP role collections to IAS user groups programmatically, saving hours of manual work, eliminating typo-induced errors, and giving you a reusable script you can run across every environment in your landscape.

Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure you have the following in place:

  • Subaccount Administrator role collection assigned to your user in the target BTP subaccount
  • A BTP subaccount with an IAS tenant configured as a custom identity provider
  • IAS user groups already created and populated with users
  • BTP CLI installed and configured
  • A REST client for testing: curl, Postman, or Bruno all work fine
  • Node.js (v18+) for the automation script (if you're creating a Node.js script like me)

 

Let's get scripting

Step 1 — Get API Credentials via the BTP CLI

To call the XSUAA REST API, you need a client credential pair. The cleanest way to get one is directly through the BTP CLI. No service instance or service key required.

btp login --sso
btp target --subaccount <SUBACCOUNT_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

Note:  This is the current recommended approach, replacing the deprecated apiaccess XSUAA service plan. If you come across older tutorials using "cf create-service xsuaa apiaccess" that approach still works but is being phased out.

The command returns a JSON object. Save these four values, you'll need all of them:

  • clientid
  • clientsecret
  • url (the token endpoint)
  • apiurl (the API base URL)

Step 2 — Get a Bearer Token

With the credentials in hand, request an OAuth token using the client credentials flow:

curl --request POST \
--url <url> \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
--data 'client_id=<clientid>' \
--data 'client_secret=<clientsecret>' \
--data 'grant_type=client_credentials' \
--data 'response_type=token'

Copy the access_token value from the response. You'll use it as a Bearer token in the next steps.

Step 3 — Check Existing Mappings (Optional but Recommended)

Before writing anything, it's worth checking what mappings already exist for your IAS identity provider. This gives you a baseline and avoids surprises:

curl --request GET \
--url <apiurl>/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/<IAS_ORIGIN_KEY>/attributes \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'authorization: Bearer <access_token>'

Where to find the IAS Origin Key: In your BTP subaccount, go to Security → Trust Configuration and click on your IAS trust entry. The Origin Key is shown in the detail panel. It typically looks like <something>.accounts.ondemand.com.

Step 4 — Create a Single Mapping

Now for the actual mapping call. Let's do one manually first to confirm everything works before running a bulk script:

curl --request POST \
--url <apiurl>/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/<IAS_ORIGIN_KEY>/attributes \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'authorization: Bearer <access_token>' \
--header 'content-type: application/json' \
--data '{
"attributeName": "Groups",
"attributeValue": "<IAS_Group_Name>",
"operator": "equals",
"roleCollectionName": "<BTP_Role_Collection_Name>"
}'

A few things to pay attention to:

  • attributeName must be exactly "Groups" with capital G, case-sensitive. This is the single most common mistake, and it fails without a helpful error message, so double-check this first.
  • attributeValue is the IAS group name, not the group ID.
  • roleCollectionName must match the role collection name exactly as it appears in the BTP cockpit.

A successful call returns HTTP 201 with the created mapping. To verify: go to BTP Cockpit → Security → Role Collections → open your role collection → User Groups tab. Your IAS group should now appear there.

Step 5 — Scale It Up: Automate with a Node.js Script

One mapping confirmed, now let's do all 130. The script below reads a list of mappings from a JSON file, fetches a token, and loops through each entry.

Project structure:

  • mappings.json – your list of group → role collection pairs
  • map-roles.mjs – the script
  • .env – credentials (never commit or publish this!)

.env

TOKEN_URL=https://<subdomain>.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/oauth/token
CLIENT_ID=<your-client-id>
CLIENT_SECRET=<your-client-secret>
API_URL=https://api.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com
IAS_ORIGIN_KEY=<your-ias-origin-key>

mappings.json

[
    {
        "iasGroup": "BTP_ADMINS",
        "roleCollection": "Subaccount Administrator"
    },
    {
        "iasGroup": "BTP_DEVELOPERS",
        "roleCollection": "Extension Developer"
    },
    {
        "iasGroup": "CPI_OPERATORS",
        "roleCollection": "PI Business Expert"
    }
]

map-roles.mjs

import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import 'dotenv/config';

const { TOKEN_URL, CLIENT_ID, CLIENT_SECRET, API_URL, IAS_ORIGIN_KEY } = process.env;

async function getToken() {
    const params = new URLSearchParams({
        grant_type: 'client_credentials',
        response_type: 'token',
        client_id: CLIENT_ID,
        client_secret: CLIENT_SECRET
    });
    const res = await fetch(TOKEN_URL, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
        body: params
    });
    const { access_token } = await res.json();
    return access_token;
}

async function mapRoleCollection(token, iasGroup, roleCollection) {
    const url = `${API_URL}/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/${IAS_ORIGIN_KEY}/attributes`;
    const res = await fetch(url, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: {
            Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
            'Content-Type': 'application/json',
            Accept: 'application/json'
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({
            attributeName: 'Groups',
            attributeValue: iasGroup,
            operator: 'equals',
            roleCollectionName: roleCollection
        })
    });

    if (res.status === 409) {
        console.log(`Already mapped: "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    if (res.status === 404) {
        console.error(`Not found (check name): "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    if (!res.ok) {
        console.error(`Failed (${res.status}): "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    console.log(`Mapped: "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
}

const mappings = JSON.parse(readFileSync('./mappings.json', 'utf-8'));
const token = await getToken();

for (const { iasGroup, roleCollection } of mappings) {
    await mapRoleCollection(token, iasGroup, roleCollection);
}

Install the one dependency and run:

npm install dotenv
node map-roles.mjs

You'll see a clear log for every mapping: success, already exists, or failure with the exact entry so you can investigate.

Bonus: Multi-Environment Reuse

Once your mappings.json is ready, deploying to multiple environments is trivial. Re-target the BTP CLI and generate a fresh set of credentials for each subaccount:

btp target --subaccount <DEV_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

# update .env, then:
node map-roles.mjs

# next subaccount 
btp target --subaccount <QA_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

# update .env, then:
node map-roles.mjs

# and so on ...

What was an 8-hour cockpit exercise becomes a 2-minute operation per environment. Repeatable, consistent, and auditable.

 

Conclusion

The SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service API is one of those tools that, once you know it's there, you'll reach for regularly. The manual cockpit approach is fine for a handful of mappings, but as soon as you're dealing with real-world project complexity with dozens of role collections, multiple environments, repeated deployments, it simply doesn't scale.

The setup described in this post takes maybe 30 minutes the first time: prepare your mappings.json, configure the .env, run one test call to validate. After that, it's just a matter of running the script. For the customer that inspired this post, what would have been a full day of clicking was done before lunch.

If you give this a try, I'd love to hear how it works for you especially if you adapt the script or extend it to cover other security artifacts. Drop a comment below or reach out directly.

Further Resources

  • Download SAP BTP CLI – https://tools.hana.ondemand.com/#cloud
  • BTP CLI Documentation – https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/sap-business-technology-platform/account-administration-using-sap-btp-command-line-interface-btp-cli
  • btp create security/api-credential – https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/btp-cli-command-reference/btp-create-security-api-credential
  • SAP Business Accelerator Hub – Authorization API – https://api.sap.com/api/AuthorizationAPI/resource/Role_collections
  • Accessing Administration APIs of SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service – https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/sap-business-technology-platform/accessing-administration-using-apis-of-sap-authorization-and-trust-management-service
  • Map Role Collections to User Groups – SAP Help – https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/sap-business-technology-platform/map-role-collections-to-user-groups

entry.title: Part 1: From OData to MCP: Building an MCP Server with SAP Integration Suite
entry.content:
Hi everyone!

Recently, I’ve been experimenting with MCP on SAP Integration Suite and looking at a practical question:

What does it actually take to make an existing enterprise API consumable by an AI client through MCP?

Rather than building an AI-specific backend, I wanted to start with something we already know well: an existing OData API.

For this experiment, I used the Business Partner (A2X) API from SAP Business Accelerator Hub and exposed selected capabilities through an MCP Server running on SAP Integration Suite’s Integration Cell runtime.

In this first part, we’ll build the provider side of the scenario:

Business Partner OData API → SAP Integration Suite / Integration Cell → MCP Server → Developer Hub

By the end of this article, we’ll have an MCP capability deployed on Integration Cell, published through Developer Hub, and ready for an MCP client to consume.

The underlying idea is important: we are not replacing the existing OData API or building a special AI backend. We are making an existing enterprise capability available to a new type of consumer through MCP.

In Part 2, we’ll take the next step: connect Joule Work Desktop as the MCP client and see what happens when the user stops thinking about OData endpoints, entities, filters, and query syntax, and simply expresses what they want in natural language.

 

 

Step-by-Step: From Business Partner OData API to MCP

Step 0: What we are building

In Part 1, we are building the provider side of the end-to-end scenario.

We’ll start with the existing Business Partner (A2X) OData API, bring it into SAP Integration Suite as an API artifact, expose selected capabilities through an MCP Server running on Integration Cell, and finally publish that MCP Server through Developer Hub.

The flow we’ll build is:

Business Partner (A2X) API
↓ OData
SAP Integration Suite / Integration Cell
↓
MCP Server
↓
Developer Hub / Product / Subscription

By the end of Part 1, the enterprise capability will be ready for an MCP client to consume.

For more background on MCP in SAP Integration Suite, see the SAP Integration Suite MCP Server documentation.

Step 1: Check the prerequisites

Before we start, make sure your SAP Integration Suite environment is ready.

For this scenario, you will need:

  • SAP Integration Suite with API Management activated
  • An active Integration Cell runtime
  • The appropriate Cloud Integration and API Management roles
  • Access to Developer Hub
  • An API that we can expose through MCP

Don't have an SAP BTP environment?

The good news is that you can also experiment with this scenario using an SAP BTP Trial account.

If you don't already have one, follow the SAP Developer tutorial Get an Account on SAP BTP Trial to set up your trial environment.

Once your SAP BTP Trial account is ready, you can continue with the SAP Integration Suite and Integration Cell setup required for this scenario.

The current SAP hands-on MCP Gateway tutorial also uses an SAP BTP Trial account as a prerequisite, so this is a convenient way to reproduce the scenario without requiring an existing productive SAP BTP landscape.

The MCP Server artifact is currently listed as available with Enhanced, Premium, Trial, and Free Tier SAP Integration Suite service plans. See Create an MCP Server for Enterprise AI Agents.

 
This means you don't necessarily need an existing productive SAP Integration Suite landscape to start experimenting with MCP.

Checkpoint

Before continuing, verify that:

✓ SAP Integration Suite is available
✓ API Management is activated
✓ Integration Cell is active
✓ You have access to Developer Hub
✓ You have an API to use for this exercise

Step 2: Find the Business Partner (A2X) API

For this demo, I wanted to start with an existing SAP business API rather than create a backend specifically for MCP.

A convenient place to explore available SAP APIs is SAP Business Accelerator Hub. The catalogue contains thousands of APIs, so it is worth being precise about which one I used for this scenario.

For this tutorial, I used:

Business Partner (A2X)
API identifier: API_BUSINESS_PARTNER

This is important because searching for “Business Partner” in SAP Business Accelerator Hub returns multiple Business Partner-related APIs and resources. To reproduce this scenario, make sure you are working with the Business Partner (A2X) API rather than another Business Partner integration.

Once you have opened the API, take a few minutes to explore its available resources and operations. For this demo, I'm interested in capabilities that support the following progression:

  1. Find Business Partners.
  2. Retrieve more information about a selected Business Partner.
  3. Present that information to the user in a useful way.

At this point, there is nothing MCP-specific about the backend. We're simply identifying the existing business capability that we eventually want our AI client to consume.

Later, when an MCP client consumes this capability, the underlying business information will still come from this existing enterprise API.

Why this matters

We're not designing an API specifically for an AI client. We're taking a business capability that already exists and introducing a new way to consume it.

Step 3: Make the API available as an API artifact on Integration Cell

Now that we have identified the API we want to expose, let's bring it into SAP Integration Suite.

Navigate to:

Integration Suite → Design → Integrations and APIs → Integration Package → Edit → Artifacts → Add → API

For details on creating API artifacts, see Create a Reusable API Artifact.

For our scenario, the result looks conceptually like this:

Business Partner API
        │
      OData
        ▼
┌───────────────────────────┐
│ SAP Integration Suite     │
│                           │
│ API artifact              │
│ Integration Cell runtime  │
└───────────────────────────┘

 

Configure backend authentication

There is one important detail in my setup.

The Business Partner API used as the backend requires an API key. Therefore, the request from the API artifact to the backend also needs to carry the appropriate backend credential.

I configured the API key on the API artifact/policy side so that the MCP consumer does not need to know or provide the backend credential.

This introduces an important distinction that we will see again later:

SAP Integration Suite
     │
     │ Backend authentication / API key
     ▼
Business Partner API
The credential used by the MCP client to access the MCP Server and the credential used by SAP Integration Suite to access the backend API serve different purposes.

Checkpoint

Before adding MCP to the picture, verify that the API artifact can successfully access the backend.

I found this separation very useful while building the demo. If the API layer works independently, any problem introduced afterwards is much easier to isolate.

Step 4: Create the MCP Server

Now we can put the MCP layer in front of the API.

In SAP Integration Suite, navigate to:

Design → Integrations and APIs → Integration Package → Artifacts → Add → MCP Server

Select the appropriate API as the source for the MCP Server.

You can find a complete example in Create an MCP Server for Enterprise AI Agents.

At this point, the architecture starts to look like this:

MCP Client
     │
     │ MCP
     ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ MCP Server              │
│                         │
│ Integration Cell        │
└────────────┬────────────┘
             │
             │ OData
             ▼
    Business Partner API
 
This is where the existing API capability starts becoming consumable through an AI-oriented interface.

Step 5: Decide what to expose through MCP

This is an important design point.

Rather than asking:

How many API operations can I expose?

I prefer to start with:

What capabilities does my MCP client actually need?

For this demo, we can work backwards from the desired conversation:

"Find business partners..."
           ↓
Need Business Partner search/retrieval

"Tell me more about the first one..."
           ↓
Need additional Business Partner details

This keeps the MCP capabilities closely aligned with the actual user scenario.

The underlying API still provides the business functions. MCP introduces a way for an AI client to discover and invoke the capabilities we choose to expose.

For additional background, see the MCP Server documentation.

Step 6: Review the MCP policy model

Before deploying the MCP Server, let's take a look at the policy model.

This is an important part of the architecture because the MCP Server doesn't simply expose the backend API directly to the AI client. The MCP request is handled through SAP Integration Suite, giving us a managed layer between the MCP consumer and the enterprise service.

For this demo, I kept the default policy model and reviewed the authentication and authorization configuration before deployment.

Conceptually, we now have:

    MCP Client
        │
       MCP
        ▼
┌──────────────────────────┐
│ SAP Integration Suite    │
│                          │
│ MCP Gateway / Policies   │
│ MCP Server               │
└────────────┬─────────────┘
             │
           OData
             ▼
    Business Partner API

The important point is that the AI client does not connect directly to the Business Partner API. SAP Integration Suite sits between the MCP consumer and the underlying enterprise capability.

Two authentication contexts

At this stage it is useful to keep the two security contexts separate:

MCP Client 
 │
 │ MCP client authentication
 │
 ▼
SAP Integration Suite
 │
 │ Backend authentication / API key
 │
 ▼
Business Partner API
We will come back to the client side of this authentication model in Part 2, when we connect Joule Work Desktop to the capability exposed here.

Step 7: Deploy the MCP Server

Now deploy the MCP Server to the Integration Cell runtime.

The server side of our architecture is now essentially complete:

┌────────────────────────────┐
│ SAP Integration Suite      │
│                            │
│ Integration Cell Runtime   │
│                            │
│      MCP Server            │
└──────────────┬─────────────┘
               │
             OData
               ▼
       Business Partner API

The SAP tutorial Create an MCP Server for Enterprise AI Agents also walks through deploying an MCP Server to Integration Cell.

Checkpoint

Before moving on, confirm that the MCP Server has been deployed successfully.

Now we have the runtime capability. The next question is how our MCP client discovers and consumes it.

Step 8: Publish the MCP Server through Developer Hub

How do I access Developer Hub?

Developer Hub is part of the API Management capabilities in SAP Integration Suite. If you haven't activated it yet, enable Developer Hub in your Integration Suite capabilities first.

Once it is activated, open the product switcher in the SAP Integration Suite header and select Developer Hub.

If you're setting this up for the first time, check the required role collections as well. For the complete setup, see Activating Developer Hub.

This was one of the most important discoveries in my own JWD test.

Once the MCP Server was running on Integration Cell, I published it through Developer Hub as part of a product.

The consumption flow becomes:

Integration Suite
      │
 MCP Server
      │
      ▼
Developer Hub
      │
   Product
      │
      ▼
MCP Consumer

In Developer Hub:

  1. Open Admin Center → Manage Content.
  2. Select the Integration Suite business system.
  3. Open the MCP Servers tab.
  4. Select the MCP Server created earlier.
  5. Choose Create Product.
  6. Provide the product name, ID, and description.
  7. Confirm that the correct MCP Server is included.
  8. Publish the product.

For the detailed publishing flow, see Discover and Publish MCP Servers from SAP Integration Suite.

For me, this step was the bridge between “I have an MCP Server running” and “I have an MCP capability that my client can actually consume.”

Step 9: Subscribe to the product

Once the product is published, subscribe to it through Developer Hub.

The end-to-end consumption flow is:

Publish MCP Server
        ↓
Publish Product
        ↓
Subscribe to Product
        ↓
Retrieve Credentials
        ↓
Configure MCP Client

This sequence turned out to be particularly important in my JWD setup.

At this point, Developer Hub is doing more than simply making the MCP Server visible. The subscription gives us the consumption information needed for the client connection.

For another end-to-end example of this flow, see Create an MCP Server for Enterprise AI Agents.

Step 10: Retrieve the client credentials

After subscribing to the product, retrieve the OAuth credentials needed by the MCP consumer.

And this is where I learned something useful.

Lesson learned from my first attempt

Initially, I tried creating credentials manually through a Process Integration Runtime Service Key.

That turned out not to be the path I needed for this scenario.

Once I published the MCP Server through Developer Hub, subscribed to the product, and used the credentials obtained through that consumption flow, the JWD connection worked.

There's also an important point in the current product documentation: the Process Integration Runtime credential approach is described as an anti-pattern, with credentials obtained through Developer Hub strongly recommended instead.

See Invoke an MCP Server Artifact by Obtaining Credentials through Process Integration Runtime.

So my practical takeaway is:

For this scenario, use the Developer Hub publication, subscription, and credential flow for the MCP client rather than starting with a manually created Process Integration Runtime Service Key.

What we have built

At this point, we have completed the provider side of the scenario:

Business Partner API → API artifact → MCP Server → Integration Cell → Developer Hub → Subscription

The existing Business Partner API remains responsible for the underlying business capability. SAP Integration Suite provides the layer through which selected capabilities are exposed via MCP, while Developer Hub provides the consumption path we will use for the MCP client.

But so far, we have only built the provider side.

The more interesting question is what happens when an AI client starts consuming that capability.

Coming next: From MCP to Natural Language

In Part 2, I'll connect Joule Work Desktop as the MCP client and move away from API terminology entirely.

Instead of thinking about endpoints or query parameters, we'll ask:

“Find business partners in Germany and show me their names and cities.”

Then we'll continue the same conversation:

“Tell me more about the first one, including its address and contact information.”

And finally:

“Summarize what we know about this business partner in a way that would be useful before a customer call.”

That's where this experiment becomes much more interesting.

entry.title: Part 2: From MCP to Natural Language: SAP Integration Suite and Joule Work Desktop
entry.content:
Hi everyone, and welcome to Part 2!

In Part 1, we started with an existing Business Partner (A2X) OData API, brought it into SAP Integration Suite as an API artifact, exposed selected capabilities through an MCP Server on Integration Cell, and published the result through Developer Hub.

Now comes the part that originally made this experiment interesting to me.

What happens when the user stops thinking about APIs and simply expresses what they want in natural language?

Our complete architecture now looks like this:

Let's connect JWD and try it.

 

 

Step 1: Connect Joule Work Desktop as the MCP client

 
If you haven't completed the MCP Server and Developer Hub setup yet, start with Part 1: From OData to MCP.

Now we can finally connect the client.

For this demo, I used Joule Work Desktop (JWD) as the MCP client and configured the connection using the MCP endpoint and OAuth information obtained through Developer Hub.

Conceptually, we have now completed the entire architecture:

Joule Work Desktop
        │
       MCP
        ▼
SAP Integration Suite
        │
   MCP Server
        │
Integration Cell Runtime
        │
      OData
        ▼
Business Partner API

Once the connector appeared as available in JWD, the configuration was behind us and I was ready to test the complete flow from the user's perspective using natural language.

This is where things become much more interesting.

Step 2: Ask the first natural-language question

Now comes the fun part.

The prompts in this example are intentionally simple.

I'm not trying to demonstrate advanced prompt engineering or prescribe a specific output format. Instead, I want to see how naturally a user can express an intent when the underlying enterprise capability is exposed through MCP.

In a production scenario, prompts could certainly be more explicit about scope, output format, constraints, and expected behaviour. For this experiment, however, I've deliberately kept them conversational.

Instead of testing the integration using API terminology, I ask JWD:

Find business partners in Germany and show me their names and cities.

What's interesting is what I didn't have to specify:

  • an OData endpoint;
  • an entity name;
  • query parameters;
  • filter syntax; or
  • a response structure.

I simply described what I wanted.

That is a very different consumption experience from working directly with an API.

But underneath that simple sentence, we are still using the Business Partner capability that we started with in Part 1.

Step 3: Continue the same conversation

The next test is deliberately not another independent API request.

I simply continue:

Tell me more about the first one, including its address and contact information.

The interesting phrase here is:

“the first one”

From the user's perspective, this is a continuation of the conversation.

There is no need to copy a Business Partner identifier from one result, work out another API operation, and construct another technical request.

The user simply expresses the next intent in the conversation.

Step 4: Move from data retrieval to business intent

Finally, I take it one step further:

Summarize what we know about this business partner in a way that would be useful before a customer call.

The progression now looks like this:

1. Find enterprise data
             │
             ▼
2. Continue conversationally
             │
             ▼
3. Turn the retrieved information
   into a user-oriented response

This is the point where, for me, the scenario becomes more interesting than simply saying “an LLM can call an API.”

We're starting with existing enterprise capabilities and changing how a user can interact with them.

Step 5: What just happened?

 
Let's return to the architecture one more time:

And this brings us back to the main point of the experiment:

The Business Partner API didn't have to become conversational.

It remains an enterprise API.

The MCP Server makes selected capabilities available through MCP, while SAP Integration Suite provides the runtime layer between the MCP consumer and the underlying enterprise service.

You can find more detail about this architecture in the SAP Integration Suite MCP documentation.

What I learned

A few things stood out to me while putting this scenario together.

1. Existing APIs become more valuable, not less

MCP doesn't mean replacing our existing REST or OData APIs.

In this scenario, the Business Partner API remains the underlying business capability. What changes is the way that capability can be exposed and consumed.

That gives our existing API investments another potential class of consumer: AI clients and agents.

2. The user experience changes dramatically

Compare the traditional API consumption process:

Understand the API
        ↓
Understand the data model
        ↓
Construct the request
        ↓
Process the response

with:

Find business partners in Germany and show me their names and cities.

The underlying business capability can remain the same while the consumer experience becomes completely different.

3. MCP authentication and backend authentication are different concerns

 

This became especially clear while building the demo.

On one side, JWD authenticates as an MCP consumer.

On the other side, Integration Suite has to authenticate when invoking the backend Business Partner API.

JWD
 │
 │ MCP authentication
 ▼
SAP Integration Suite
 │
 │ Backend authentication
 ▼
Business Partner API

Keeping these two concerns separate made the architecture, and the troubleshooting, much clearer.

4. Developer Hub was the missing piece for my JWD connection

 

My initial attempt focused too much on creating credentials directly.

The successful path was:

Deploy → Publish through Developer Hub → Subscribe → Retrieve credentials → Connect JWD

Once I followed that consumption model, the pieces came together.

Closing thoughts

For me, this is where MCP starts to get really interesting.

The exciting part isn't that an AI client can execute an HTTP request. It's that we can take business capabilities that already exist, selectively expose them through MCP, and let users interact with those capabilities in terms of intent rather than API implementation.

The Business Partner API remains an API.

What changed is how the capability is discovered, invoked, and experienced by the user.

And that raises an interesting question for integration architects:

As AI clients become another consumer of enterprise capabilities, how should we design, expose, secure, and govern the APIs behind them?

I'd love to hear how others are exploring MCP in their own integration scenarios. If you've tried connecting MCP clients to SAP Integration Suite, or have a different approach to exposing enterprise APIs to AI clients, please share your experience, questions, or lessons learned in the comments below. Let's learn from each other!

entry.title: SAP BAIP Kyma runtime 正式落地中国：扩展云原生开发能力
entry.content:
SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime 现已在中国正式上线，在本地 SAP BAIP 上提供了一个托管 Kubernetes 运行时，支持云原生应用、微服务及 SAP 扩展开发。

云原生创新能力走近中国客户

现代企业越来越需要在不增加核心系统复杂度的前提下，扩展业务应用、连接各类系统、并持续交付新的数字化能力。

SAP BAIP 在中国已提供 Cloud Foundry runtime 作为成熟的 PaaS 选项，适用于基于 buildpack 工作流的应用部署。Kyma runtime 则面向不同的需求场景。它基于开源 Kyma 项目和 Kubernetes 构建，让开发团队可以直接使用容器化工作负载、Serverless Functions 以及更广泛的 Kubernetes 生态系统——不限编程语言和框架。任何可容器化的工作负载均可在 Kyma runtime 上运行。

2026 年 6 月 2 日，SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime 在中国（华北3）率先上线，随后于 2026 年 7 月 10 日扩展至中国（上海）——通过本地 BTPEA 商业模式，在两个区域全面开放。

现已提供哪些内容？

该服务基于 BTPEA 商业模式提供，SKU 为 8016044（面向客户的 BTPEA SKU），包含以下服务计划：

服务名称服务计划名称可用数据中心
Kyma RuntimeKyma Runtime Alibaba Cloud中国（上海）— cn40
Kyma RuntimeKyma Runtime Azure中国（华北3）— cn20

客户和合作伙伴可通过 SAP Discovery Center 查看服务及其可用地区：

  • 中国（华北3）— Kyma runtime
  • 中国（上海）— Kyma runtime

中国 BTPEA 价格表中列出了 SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime 的 Standard 计费计划。

为何重要

托管、灵活的云原生应用基础平台

自建 Kubernetes 需要持续投入集群管理、版本升级、安全补丁和基础设施运维。SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime 消除了这一负担：SAP 负责底层平台的管理，客户则完全掌控自己的应用和工作负载。开发团队可以专注于构建业务能力，而不是维护基础设施。

与 Cloud Foundry runtime 相比，Kyma 提供了一种截然不同的开发模式。Cloud Foundry 通过 buildpack 对运行时进行抽象，这种方式非常适合快速部署 Java 或 Node.js 应用，但对能运行什么、如何运行有一定限制。Kyma 没有这类约束：无论使用何种语言或框架，任何容器化工作负载都可以在 Kyma 上运行，团队还可以直接使用 Kubernetes 原生工具链——包括用于打包的 Helm、自定义资源定义、精细化资源配置，以及更广泛的 CNCF 生态系统。对于构建现代云原生应用或需要精确控制工作负载的团队而言，这种灵活性是显著的优势。

两种运行时相辅相成。Cloud Foundry 仍然是 buildpack 应用部署的可靠选择；当团队需要容器原生的灵活性、多语言支持或 Kubernetes 生态工具时，Kyma 则更为适合。

通过事件驱动集成扩展 SAP 应用

Kyma runtime 内置了 Eventing 组件，允许应用直接订阅来自 SAP S/4HANA 及其他 SAP 系统的业务事件——扩展程序可以实时响应销售订单创建、货物移动或主数据变更等事件，无需轮询或点对点连接。由于该能力已集成在运行时中，团队无需单独配置消息服务即可开始构建事件驱动扩展。

结合 Serverless Functions 和内置 API Gateway，这使得构建轻量、松耦合的扩展程序变得切实可行——这些扩展与 SAP 核心系统并行运行，而非嵌入其中。自定义逻辑独立演进，升级周期解耦，核心系统保持稳定。

对于超出 SAP 间集成范畴的场景——连接第三方系统、编排多步骤工作流或构建全新业务应用——Kyma 提供了同样的 Kubernetes 基础平台，并具备灵活引入任何所需服务或技术的能力。

扩展本地 SAP BAIP 开发组合

随着 Kyma runtime 在中国（华北3）和中国（上海）相继上线，中国客户在 SAP BAIP 上多了一个可用的运行时选择。

对于正在构建容器化应用、API 集成、事件驱动扩展或微服务的团队，这一选项尤为实用。

Kyma runtime 的上线拓宽了中国生态系统可用的技术选择，为云原生应用开发提供了又一个坚实基础。

entry.title: Bringing SAP BAIP, Kyma Runtime to China: Expanding Cloud-Native Development Capabilities
entry.content:
SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime is now available in China, extending the local SAP BAIP portfolio with a managed Kubernetes-based runtime for cloud-native applications, microservices, and SAP extensions.

Bringing Cloud-Native Innovation Closer to Chinese Customers

Modern enterprises increasingly need to extend business applications, connect systems, and deliver new digital capabilities without introducing unnecessary complexity into their core landscapes.

SAP BAIP in China already offers Cloud Foundry runtime as a mature PaaS option for deploying applications using buildpack-based workflows. Kyma runtime addresses a different set of needs. Built on the open-source Kyma project and Kubernetes, it gives development teams direct access to container-based workloads, serverless functions, and the broader Kubernetes ecosystem—without restriction on programming language or framework. Any workload that can be containerized can run on Kyma runtime.

On June 2, 2026, SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime became available in China (North 3), followed by China (Shanghai) on July 10, 2026—making this managed cloud-native application runtime available through the local BTPEA commercial offering across both regions.

What Is Now Available?

  • China (Shanghai) — Kyma Runtime

Why This Matters

A Managed, Flexible Foundation for Cloud-Native Applications

Running Kubernetes in-house requires ongoing investment in cluster management, upgrades, security patching, and infrastructure operations. SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime removes that burden: SAP manages the underlying platform, while customers retain full control over their applications and workloads. Development teams can focus on building business capabilities instead of maintaining infrastructure.

Compared to Cloud Foundry runtime, Kyma offers a meaningfully different development model. Cloud Foundry abstracts the runtime through buildpacks, which works well for deploying Java or Node.js applications quickly but limits what you can run and how. Kyma places no such constraints: any containerized workload runs on Kyma regardless of language or framework, and teams have direct access to Kubernetes-native tooling—Helm for packaging, custom resource definitions, fine-grained resource configuration, and the broader CNCF ecosystem. For teams building modern cloud-native applications or needing precise control over their workloads, this flexibility is a significant advantage.

The two runtimes are complementary. Cloud Foundry remains a solid choice for buildpack-based application deployment; Kyma is the better fit when container-native flexibility, polyglot development, or Kubernetes ecosystem tooling is a requirement.

Extending SAP Applications with Event-Driven Integration

Kyma runtime includes a built-in Eventing component that allows applications to subscribe directly to business events from SAP S/4HANA and other SAP systems—so an extension can react to a sales order creation, a goods movement, or a master data change in real time, without polling or point-to-point connections. Having this capability integrated into the runtime means teams can start building event-driven extensions without separately provisioning and configuring a messaging service.

Combined with serverless functions and a built-in API Gateway, this makes it practical to build lightweight, loosely coupled extensions that sit alongside the SAP core rather than inside it. Custom logic evolves independently, upgrade cycles are decoupled, and the core system remains stable.

For scenarios that go beyond SAP-to-SAP integration—connecting third-party systems, orchestrating multi-step workflows, or building net-new business applications—Kyma provides the same Kubernetes-based foundation with the flexibility to incorporate any service or technology the use case requires.

Expanding the Local SAP BAIP Development Portfolio

With Kyma runtime available in China (North 3) and China (Shanghai), customers gain an additional runtime option within the local SAP BAIP portfolio.

This is particularly relevant for teams building containerized applications, API-based integrations, event-driven extensions, and microservices that complement SAP business solutions.

The availability of Kyma runtime broadens the technology choices available to the China ecosystem and provides another foundation for cloud-native application development.

entry.title: Part 2 of 2 – Securing AI-Powered SAP Apps on SAP BTP: Single Sign-On and Role-Based Access with XSU
entry.content:
Overview

Part 1 of this series described how SAP S/4HANA data can be made available to AI clients through an MCP server running on SAP BTP. Once such data is exposed through a user interface, the application must meet the same security standards as any other access to SAP systems.

This article describes how a UI application on SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry runtime, authenticates users and enforces authorizations using two standard platform components:

  • Application router – the single entry point that handles user login and request forwarding.
  • SAP Authorization and Trust Management service (XSUAA) – the service that issues tokens and manages scopes, role templates and role collections.

The approach addresses three requirements:

  • Authentication: only users with a valid corporate identity can access the application.
  • Authorization: each user can access only the functions assigned to them.
  • Enforcement: authorization decisions are made on the server and cannot be bypassed in the browser.

Solution components

Component Responsibility

Identity provider (for example, SAP Cloud Identity Services connected to the corporate directory)Authenticates the user through corporate single sign-on.
XSUAAIssues a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) containing the user's scopes, based on the assigned role collections.
Application routerActs as the single public entry point. Redirects unauthenticated users to the login, maintains the user session and forwards requests to the application together with the token.
UI applicationValidates the token on every request and grants access only to the functions permitted by its scopes.

Users always access the application through the application router, and the application validates the token independently. This provides two separate layers of control.

Authentication flow

The following steps describe the first access of a user to the application:

  1. The browser requests the application through the application router. No session exists yet.
  2. The application router redirects the request to XSUAA, which delegates authentication to the configured identity provider.
  3. The user authenticates with the corporate login, typically through single sign-on.
  4. The identity provider confirms the user's identity to XSUAA. XSUAA determines the user's role collections and issues a JWT containing the corresponding scopes.
  5. The application router stores the token in its server-side session and returns the requested page. The browser receives only a session cookie.
  6. For each subsequent request, the application router attaches the token and forwards the request to the application.
  7. The application validates the token (signature, expiry and audience) and evaluates the scopes before processing the request.

 

Figure 1: Authentication flow. The highlighted arrows show where the token is transferred; it is exchanged only between server-side components.

When the session expires, the application router repeats the flow from step 2.

Authorization model

XSUAA separates the definition of permissions from their assignment through three levels:

Level Purpose Maintained by

ScopeA single permission that the application checksDeveloper, in xs-security.json
Role templateGroups one or more scopes into a functional roleDeveloper, in xs-security.json
Role collectionBundles roles for assignment to users or user groupsAdministrator, in the SAP BTP cockpit

The complete xs-security.json is shown in step 1 of the configuration below.

With this model, access is managed entirely in the SAP BTP cockpit. Granting or revoking access requires no code change and no redeployment. Assigning role collections to user groups from the identity provider, rather than to individual users, keeps access aligned with organizational changes automatically.

Configuration steps

The following examples use generic names (my-xsuaa, my-approuter, my-ui-app) and placeholders in angle brackets. Replace them with the values of your own subaccount.

Step 1: Define the security descriptor (xs-security.json)

{
  "xsappname": "my-ui-app",
  "tenant-mode": "dedicated",
  "scopes": [
    { "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Display", "description": "Use the application" },
    { "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Monitor", "description": "Use the monitoring functions" }
  ],
  "role-templates": [
    { "name": "Viewer",         "scope-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.Display"] },
    { "name": "MonitoringUser", "scope-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.Display", "$XSAPPNAME.Monitor"] }
  ],
  "role-collections": [
    { "name": "App Viewers",      "role-template-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.Viewer"] },
    { "name": "Monitoring Users", "role-template-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.MonitoringUser"] }
  ],
  "oauth2-configuration": {
    "redirect-uris": ["https://<approuter-host>.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/**"]
  }
}

Create the XSUAA service instance from this file. Later changes are applied to the same instance with update-service:

cf create-service xsuaa application my-xsuaa -c xs-security.json
cf update-service my-xsuaa -c xs-security.json

Step 2: Configure the application router

The application router is a small Node.js application based on the @SAP/approuter package. It needs three files.

package.json:

{
  "name": "my-approuter",
  "dependencies": { "@sap/approuter": "^20" },
  "scripts": { "start": "node node_modules/@sap/approuter/approuter.js" }
}

xs-app.json – every route requires an XSUAA login, and requests are forwarded to the UI application:

{
  "welcomeFile": "/",
  "authenticationMethod": "route",
  "logout": { "logoutEndpoint": "/logout" },
  "routes": [
    {
      "source": "^/(.*)$",
      "target": "/$1",
      "destination": "ui-app",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    }
  ]
}

manifest.yml – the destination ui-app points to the UI application, and forwardAuthToken passes the user's token on:

applications:
  - name: my-approuter
    memory: 256M
    services:
      - my-xsuaa
    env:
      destinations: >
        [ { "name": "ui-app",
            "url": "https://<ui-app-host>.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com",
            "forwardAuthToken": true } ]

Set csrfProtection according to your application. If the UI application implements its own CSRF protection, the router's protection can be switched off for its routes, as shown above.

Step 3: Bind XSUAA to the UI application

The UI application needs the same XSUAA instance to validate the tokens it receives. Add it to the application's manifest.yml:

applications:
  - name: my-ui-app
    services:
      - my-xsuaa

Deploy both applications:

cf push my-ui-app
cf push my-approuter

Step 4: Configure trust and assign roles

In the SAP BTP cockpit, open Security → Trust Configuration and establish trust with your identity provider. Then assign the role collections under Security → Role Collections, preferably to user groups. With the SAP BTP command line interface, the assignment can also be scripted:

btp assign security/role-collection "Monitoring Users" --to-user <user@example.com>

Server-side authorization checks

The application router ensures that only authenticated users reach the application. Fine-grained authorization is performed by the application itself, on the server, for every request:

  1. Validate the forwarded token and reject requests with a missing, expired or foreign token.
  2. Read the scopes from the token.
  3. Expose only the functions and data permitted by those scopes, both in the user interface and in the server's API responses.

Because these checks run on the server, they cannot be circumvented by modifying the page or by calling the application's API directly.

For Node.js applications, SAP provides the @SAP/xssec and @SAP/xsenv packages for token validation. A minimal example with Express:

const express = require("express");
const xsenv = require("@sap/xsenv");
const { XsuaaService, createSecurityContext } = require("@sap/xssec");

const xsuaa = new XsuaaService(xsenv.getServices({ xsuaa: { tag: "xsuaa" } }).xsuaa);
const app = express();

// 1. Validate the token on every request
app.use(async (req, res, next) => {
  try {
    req.authInfo = await createSecurityContext(xsuaa, { req });
    next();
  } catch (e) {
    res.status(401).json({ error: "Not authenticated" });
  }
});

// 2. Require a scope for a protected function
const requireScope = (scope) => (req, res, next) =>
  req.authInfo.checkLocalScope(scope) ? next() : res.status(403).json({ error: "Not authorized" });

app.get("/api/monitoring", requireScope("Monitor"), (req, res) => {
  res.json({ status: "ok" });   // only reached with the Monitor scope
});

app.listen(process.env.PORT || 8080);

For Java applications, the SAP Cloud Security Services Integration Library (java-security) offers the same functions.

Backend connectivity

User authentication protects access to the application. Communication between the application and SAP S/4HANA is a separate, technical connection through an SAP BTP destination and the SAP Cloud Connector, using a technical user. As a result, SAP S/4HANA authorizes the technical user rather than the individual end user.

This is suitable for a proof of concept. For productive use, principal propagation should be considered, so that the end user's own SAP authorizations are also applied in the backend system.

Handling session expiry in the UI

When the application router session expires, background requests (for example fetch calls) receive a login redirect or an HTTP 401 instead of data. A reload of the page lets the application router restart the authentication flow:

async function callApi(url, options) {
  const res = await fetch(url, { credentials: "include", ...options });
  const isJson = (res.headers.get("content-type") || "").includes("application/json");
  if (res.status === 401 || !isJson) {
    window.location.reload();        // the application router redirects to the login
    return null;
  }
  return res.json();
}

Key considerations

Topic Consideration

Role changesScopes are written into the token at login. After a role collection is assigned or removed, the user must log in again for the change to take effect.
Session expiryBackground requests cannot complete an interactive login. When a session expires, the application should reload the page so that the application router can restart the authentication flow.
Service updatesUpdates to the XSUAA instance must be applied with the intended xs-security.json. Verify the resulting roles in the SAP BTP cockpit after each update.
Client-side restrictionsHiding functions in the user interface does not replace server-side authorization checks.
CredentialsTechnical credentials, such as API keys, should be provided through service bindings rather than environment variables or source code.

Summary

The application router and XSUAA provide a UI application on SAP BTP with the same authentication and authorization model as any other SAP BTP application:

  • A single entry point with corporate single sign-on.
  • Permissions carried in a signed token, defined by developers and assigned by administrators.
  • Authorization decisions enforced on the server.

An application that exposes SAP data through AI therefore requires no dedicated security model; it integrates into the standard security concept of SAP BTP. Principal propagation is the logical next step to extend user-specific authorizations to the SAP backend.

entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 3: Second Content Agent and target in Central
entry.content:
Part 3 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent.

In Part 2 we set up Dev, so a parcel can now be packed and dropped at the source node. In this part we build the receiving end in Central: a second Content Agent that unpacks the parcel, the connection CTMS uses to reach it, and the connection it uses to write into the target Integration Suite.

 

Before you start

The target Integration Suite runs in Central, with the Cloud Integration capability activated (the same rule as in Dev).

Step 1: Process Integration Runtime instance and key

Same as in Dev: an instance of SAP Process Integration Runtime, plan api, with the roles WorkspacePackagesRead, WorkspacePackagesEdit and WorkspacePackagesTransport, and a service key. This time it gives the unpacker access to the target workspace.

Step 2: The second Content Agent

  • Create an instance of Content Agent service with the application plan and the role Import. This is the unpacker.
  • Create a service key. You need its url and, from the uaa section, clientid, clientsecret and url.

Step 3: CloudIntegration destination in Central

The unpacker writes into Integration Suite through a destination named CloudIntegration, filled exactly like the Dev one in Part 2, but from the key of step 1. You can also let the Content Agent UI create it for you when you activate the Cloud Integration content type (see "What tripped me up" first).

Step 4: The transport destination CTMS uses

CTMS needs to know where to deliver the parcel. In Central, create a destination for that. Its name is free; I used CAS_on_target.

FieldValue
URLurl from the Content Agent key (step 2)
AuthenticationOAuth2ClientCredentials
Client ID / secretclientid / clientsecret from the uaa section
Token Service URLurl from the uaa section + /oauth/token

Step 5: Finish the target node

Open CTMS, edit the target node from Part 1 and pick CAS_on_target as its destination. The content type stays Multi-Target Application.

 

The target node with its content type and destination.

A green Check Connection on CAS_on_target only proves the address is reachable (Part 2 explains why). The real test is the first transport in Part 4.

What tripped me up in my setup

  • Three identical runtime instances. Central had three Process Integration Runtime instances with the same name, each in a different Cloud Foundry space, left over from earlier attempts. Before copying a key I had to check which space the target Cloud Integration actually runs in, and use the instance from that space. Clear names would have saved me this.
  • Activating the content type failed because the destination already existed. Activating the Cloud Integration content type in the Content Agent UI creates a CloudIntegration destination for you. I had already created one by hand, so the activation did not go through. It also asks for a Cloud Foundry passcode, and I first suspected the login URL and changed it to the Cloud Foundry API endpoint, which changed nothing. The fix was simple: I edited my existing CloudIntegration destination, added the client secret, and the activation went through. Either create the destination by hand or let the Content Agent UI do it, not both.

Roles for this part

Instance roles only: the three Workspace roles on the runtime instance and Import on the Content Agent instance. The user roles come in Part 4, and Part 7 lists them all.

What comes next

Both ends are now connected. In Part 4 we switch on Transport in Integration Suite, send the first package and import it in CTMS, including the role that kept the Transport option greyed out for me.

entry.title: Calling On-Premise Systems from Go on SAP BTP: Bindings, Tunnels and Destinations
entry.content:
The problem

While building a small Go service on SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry runtime, that had to reach two things behind an SAP Cloud Connector: an SFTP server and an OData v2 service. Before any business logic, there were three small problems to solve:

  1. Where are my credentials? On Cloud Foundry they are in VCAP_SERVICES. On SAP BTP, Kyma runtime they are files in the pod.
  2. How do I get a TCP connection through the Connectivity service? Its SOCKS5 proxy uses a login method specific to SAP.
  3. How do I turn a Destination service entry into a client I can call? The destination describes the target, but you still have to apply it yourself.

Below is how each one was solved. I'm assuming you already know how to create and bind the Destination, Connectivity and Authorization and Trust Management (XSUAA) service instances and map a virtual host in Cloud Connector.

1. Reading bindings without caring where you run

The code that reads credentials shouldn't change between Cloud Foundry and Kyma. I put both behind one small interface, with a detector that picks the right one at startup:

prov, err := auto.NewProvider()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

cb, err := binding.Connectivity(prov, "") // proxy host and ports, client id/secret
db, err := binding.Destination(prov, "")  // Destination service URI and credentials

An empty name takes the first binding of that type; pass an instance name if you have several. Detection checks VCAP_SERVICES first, then SERVICE_BINDING_ROOT, then whether a /bindings directory exists.

2. A tunnel through the Connectivity service

The Connectivity service offers a SOCKS5 proxy. Instead of the usual username/password, it expects an SAP-specific authentication method (0x80) in which you send a JWT from XSUAA. The standard library and golang.org/x/net/proxy don't implement it, so I wrote it.

You give the dialer a token source (client-credentials tokens, cached until shortly before they expire) and the proxy details from the binding:

connSrc := xsuaa.NewClientCredentialsSource(xsuaa.Config{
    ClientID:     cb.ClientID,
    ClientSecret: cb.ClientSecret,
    TokenURL:     cb.TokenServiceURL + "/oauth/token",
})

dialer := connectivity.NewDialer(connectivity.Config{
    ProxyHost:   cb.OnpremiseProxyHost,
    ProxyPort:   cb.OnpremiseProxySocks5Port,
    TokenSource: connSrc,
})

conn, err := dialer.Dial(ctx, "internal-sftp.corp", 22, "")

The host and port must match a virtual mapping in Cloud Connector; the last argument is the Cloud Connector location ID (empty means the default location). You get back a plain net.Conn, so SSH, TLS or anything else can run on top.

Gotcha: when a dial fails, the error is a *connectivity.StageError that says whether it failed at dial, greeting, auth or connect. That tells you quickly whether to look at the token or at Cloud Connector access control.

For SFTP I also added sshclient.Dial, a thin wrapper that builds the SSH config from the destination and retries handshake failures with backoff.

3. From a Destination to a working HTTP client

Destination lookups use the same token pattern, built from the destination binding:

destSrc := xsuaa.NewClientCredentialsSource(xsuaa.Config{
    ClientID:     db.ClientID,
    ClientSecret: db.ClientSecret,
    TokenURL:     db.TokenServiceURL + "/oauth/token",
})
destClient := destination.NewClient(db.URI, destSrc, nil)

dest, err := destClient.Find(ctx, "MY_HTTP_DEST")

Then httpclient.New turns the destination into an *http.Client that applies its authentication and, for OnPremise destinations, routes through the Connectivity service's HTTP proxy:

cfg := httpclient.Config{}
if strings.EqualFold(dest.ProxyType, "OnPremise") {
    cfg.HTTPProxy = &httpclient.HTTPProxyConfig{Binding: cb}
}
client, baseURL, err := httpclient.New(dest, cfg)

resp, err := client.Get(baseURL + "/sap/opu/odata/sap/MY_SERVICE/Items?$top=5")

Gotcha: OData v2 writes need an X-CSRF-Token that is tied to a session cookie. The client keeps a cookie jar for that, and a helper fetches the token:

csrf, err := httpclient.FetchCSRF(ctx, client, baseURL+"/")
req.Header.Set("X-CSRF-Token", csrf) // then client.Do(req) for the POST

What it doesn't do

  • Client-credentials only. No principal propagation or user token exchange; everything runs as your service binding's technical client.
  • Secret-based bindings only. Bindings that use X.509 certificates instead of a client secret aren't handled.
  • sshclientskips SSH host-key checking by default. You can pass your own HostKeyCallback, and in anything beyond a demo you should.
  • Tested against fakes. The unit tests use local fake proxies and httptest servers, not a real Connectivity service, Destination service or Cloud Connector. [Author: state exactly what you have run end to end, e.g. whether you ran the Kyma path on a real cluster.]
  • Not an SAP product. It's an independent project, not provided or endorsed by SAP. It relies on service behaviour as I understood it from SAP's documentation and from observation, so check it against the current documentation for your landscape.

Quick start

The repository has three runnable Cloud Foundry examples (examples/sftp-count, examples/sftp-sshclient, examples/http-odata), each with a manifest and README. For the OData one:

cf create-service xsuaa application my-xsuaa
cf create-service connectivity lite my-connectivity
cf create-service destination lite my-destination

cd examples/http-odata
cf push
curl "https://<app-route>/odata?destination=MY_HTTP_DEST&path=/Items?%24top=5"

It needs Go 1.25 or later. Apart from sshclient, which uses golang.org/x/crypto, the packages use only the standard library, and there are no SAP-published Go dependencies. On my machine (Go 1.25.10, macOS arm64) go test -cover reports between about 70% and 94% statement coverage per module; that measures what the fakes exercise, not behaviour against real systems.

It's open source under the Apache License 2.0 at https://github.com/bluefunda/btp-go, with API docs at https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/bluefunda/btp-go. Several modules are still v0.x, so expect the API to change. Corrections are welcome, especially from anyone who has seen the Connectivity proxy behave differently in another landscape or on Kyma.

entry.title: Use SAP AI Core Models in VS Code Chat Without a Copilot Plan
entry.content:
VS Code’s Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) support lets developers use provider backed models in Chat without a Copilot plan. That can be useful when a team already has access to models through SAP AI Core and wants to work with them in VS Code.

There’s a small integration challenge with SAP AI Core service keys: they contain OAuth credentials and service URLs, not a standard model API key you can paste into a generic endpoint form. The client needs to exchange these credentials for an access token, then use that token and the correct resource group to make model requests.

I built SAPilot to handle those steps and make supported SAP AI Core deployments available in the VS Code Chat model picker.

What happens between Connect and Chat

After you enter your service key details, SAPilot stores the client secret in VS Code’s SecretStorage. The client ID, authentication URL, AI Core API URL, and resource group are stored separately as nonsecret connection settings. When SAPilot needs to call SAP AI Core, it requests an OAuth access token using the client credentials flow. The token is cached until shortly before it expires.

The exchange is the part that makes a service key different from a simple API key. This shortened example shows the same basic request SAPilot makes:

let tokenUrl = authUrl;
if (!tokenUrl.endsWith('/oauth/token')) tokenUrl += '/oauth/token';

const response = await fetch(`${tokenUrl}?grant_type=client_credentials`, {
  method: 'POST',
  redirect: 'error',
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Basic ${Buffer.from(`${clientId}:${clientSecret}`).toString('base64')}`
  }
});

if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`SAP sign-in failed: ${response.status}`);
const { access_token: accessToken, expires_in: expiresIn } = await response.json();

For a chat request, SAPilot sends the access token as a bearer token and adds the AI-Resource-Group header. It also discovers running deployments and chooses a compatible request format for each supported chat model. This is why connecting SAP AI Core takes more than entering a base URL and a key.

A small security decision with a practical effect

A design choice was where to persist the values entered during setup. SAPilot uses VS Code’s SecretStorage for the client secret and globalState for the client ID and endpoint details. VS Code documents SecretStorage as encrypted storage for sensitive values, while extension state is intended for ordinary key-value data. Keeping the secret out of ordinary configuration avoids writing it alongside nonsecret settings.

This choice also affects setup: the secret is stored locally through VS Code and is not synced between machines, so you enter it again on another machine. SAPilot never needs a shared credential embedded in the extension; each developer connects using their own service key. Prompts and chat context are sent to the SAP AI Core model selected in Chat, so the model and service key should be chosen according to your organization’s data and access policies.

Why use the Chat Provider API?

VS Code’s Language Model Chat Provider API lets an extension contribute models to the existing picker and handle requests for them. SAPilot registers a provider, looks up deployments available to the connected service key, and returns the supported chat deployments to VS Code. When you select one, the extension translates the chat messages into that model’s request format and streams the response back into Chat.

That provider layer is useful here because SAP AI Core can expose different model families and request formats. SAPilot currently handles supported OpenAI compatible Chat Completions, Claude, Bedrock Converse, Cohere Chat, and Gemini on Vertex AI deployments. Deployments that are not supported chat models, such as embeddings, are left out of the picker.

The result is a familiar workflow: connect once, open Chat, and select an SAP AI Core deployment. You do not need to copy an access token into VS Code or manually add a resource-group header for every request.

Getting started and scope

Install SAPilot in VS Code 1.104 or later, run SAPilot: Connect to SAP AI Core, and enter your service key details. You need permission to use a running chat deployment. Then open Chat and select a model under SAP AI Core.

BYOK makes this chat workflow available without a Copilot plan, but model usage still follows the billing terms of your SAP AI Core account. Some VS Code capabilities, including inline suggestions and semantic search, remain tied to GitHub or Copilot services. Model cost, quality, and speed depend on the deployment, usage, and task.

A takeaway and what’s next

SAPilot shows how VS Code’s BYOK support can connect developers to models their organization already provides through SAP AI Core. BYOK changes which service handles chat requests; model usage still follows your SAP AI Core billing and your organization’s data policies. If you try SAPilot, have a question, or would like to suggest a feature, let me know in the comments. You can also contribute by raising a pull request on GitHub.

References

  • Use your own language model key in VS Code
  • VS Code Language Model Chat Provider API
  • VS Code extension data storage and SecretStorage
  • SAP AI Core: Use a Service Key
  • SAPilot source code

entry.title: From Integration to Intelligence :Building enterprise-ready AI agents with Integration Suite & MCP
entry.content:
I have sat through a lot of agent demos this year. The pattern is usually the same. Someone types a request in plain English, the agent reads a purchase requisition, checks a budget, creates a purchase order in S/4HANA, emails the supplier, and posts a cheerful summary. The room claps. It is impressive.

Then I ask the question that integration people always ask: what happens on the 40,000th run? What happens when the supplier endpoint times out, when the mapping changes, when audit wants to know who approved what, or when the token bill arrives at the end of the month?

That is the gap between an agent that works in a demo and an agent that survives production. After close to two decades of building integrations, first on Oracle SOA and OSB, later on Boomi, Apigee and SAP BTP, my view is that the gap is mostly not a model problem. It is an architecture problem. And it is one the SAP integration community is unusually well placed to solve.

Last week I attended SAP's session "Building the Autonomous Enterprise with Integration Suite, AEM, and Agents" (13 October 2026). One line from it has stayed with me, because it captures the whole argument in eight words:

"Let the agent think. Let Integration Suite execute."

This post is my attempt to unpack that line from an architect's point of view: where agents earn their keep, where they should stay out of the way, and how API-centric integration and the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite connect the two.

1. The overloaded agent

When teams first build agents, they tend to give them everything. The agent calls the APIs, builds the payloads, decides on retries, transforms the formats and handles the errors. It feels efficient because there is only one component to think about.

It is not efficient. In effect you are asking a probabilistic reasoning engine to re-implement things your integration platform already does deterministically, with monitoring, retries and audit built in. Mapping JSON to IDoc, routing a message by company code, validating mandatory fields against a schema, sending a payment file over a bank channel: none of these need judgment. They need to be done exactly the same way every time.

The SAP session framed the consequences well, and they match what I have seen in practice:

  • Duplicated capability. The agent rebuilds APIs, EDI handling, mappings and routing you already own.
  • Reduced reliability. Predictable PO, invoice and payment flows start to depend on non-deterministic behavior.
  • Harder governance. Security, auditability and compliance become difficult to standardize when logic lives inside prompts.
  • Blurred accountability. When something fails, is it the reasoning, the integration, the partner or the backend? Nobody can tell quickly.
  • Higher operating cost. Tokens and agent capacity are spent on repetitive plumbing instead of the reasoning you actually wanted.

I like to describe it as driving a Lamborghini to the supermarket. You can, but it is not what the car is for, and the parking is a nightmare.

2. Who should own each step? A Procure-to-Pay test

The most useful part of the session, for me, was a simple step-by-step assessment of a standard Procure-to-Pay flow. For each step, it asked one question: is the value here in reasoning, or in reliable execution? I have adapted it below because I think every team should run this exercise on its own processes before writing a single prompt.

#

P2P step

Owner

Why

1

Agent

2

Low

High

Agent

Summarize context and policy, recommend

3

Create purchase order

Very high

Integration Suite

Structured execution: APIs, EDI, mapping

4

Very high

Integration Suite

Receive, transform, update

5

6

7
